chunks: And beware of showing obligation on your subjects for your good deeds,
or self-praise regarding what you have done, or making promises to them and then following your promise with breaking it.
For showing obligation destroys the good deed, self-praise takes away the light of truth, and breaking promises earns hatred before Allah and the people.
Allah the Glorified says: "Most hateful is it unto Allah that you say what you do not do."

key_terms.التَّزَيُّدَ: Self-praise or exaggerating one's own good deeds
key_terms.الْخُلْفَ: Breaking a promise or going back on one's word
key_terms.الْمَنَّ: Showing obligation or reminding of favors to diminish the value of a good deed
key_terms.رَعِيَّتِكَ: Your subjects or people under your governance

ai.seo_question: What are the three ethical pitfalls for leaders mentioned in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this foundational directive from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali outlines the ethical governance principles for Malik al-Ashtar, warning that ingratitude for favors (al-mann) nullifies virtue, while self-aggrandizement (al-tazayud) obscures divine truth. The text emphasizes that breaking promises (al-khulf) incurs divine wrath, linking political integrity directly to spiritual accountability in the Shia tradition of just rule.
